# Convert WAV to MP3

- Route: `/tools/convert-wav-to-mp3`
- Kind: `tool`
- Category: `audio`
- Slug: `convert-wav-to-mp3`

## Summary

Shrink large lossless WAV recordings into widely compatible MP3 files for podcasts, sharing, and storage. (Audio tools)

## Details

WAV files are lossless and large. MP3 is the universally compatible compressed audio format — every phone, laptop, and music app plays it. Media Manipulator re-encodes your WAV to MP3 at the bitrate you pick, so you trade only a tiny bit of quality for a 5–10× smaller file.
### What it does
- Re-encodes WAV recordings to MP3 at your chosen bitrate.
- Supports custom sample rates, channels, and bitrate (128 to 320 kbps).
- Preserves loudness and avoids unnecessary re-resampling.
- Outputs a standard ID3-tagged .mp3 file.
### How to use it
1. Upload WAV: Drop in any .wav file from your computer.
2. Pick bitrate: 192 kbps for voice, 256–320 kbps for music.
3. Encode MP3: FFmpeg encodes a clean MP3 at the chosen settings.
4. Download MP3: Save a widely compatible .mp3.
### Technical details
- Uses LAME-style encoding via FFmpeg under the hood.
- MP3 is a lossy codec — quality plateaus around 256 kbps for music. Voice content sounds great at 128–192 kbps.
- If you need lossless smaller files, use FLAC or ALAC instead. Use Opus (in OGG) for the smallest modern lossy files when you control the player.
### Use cases
- Podcast episodes: Master in WAV, publish as MP3 at 96–128 kbps mono.
- Voice memos: Shrink phone recordings before sharing or archiving.
- Music demos: Send mixes at 256–320 kbps without huge attachment sizes.
- Embedding on a website: Use MP3 for compatibility — every browser plays it natively.
### FAQ
Q: What bitrate should I pick?
A: 192 kbps is a balanced default. Use 128 kbps for voice/podcast, 256–320 kbps for music.
Q: Will the audio quality drop?
A: Slightly — MP3 is lossy. At 256+ kbps most listeners cannot tell the difference from the WAV original.
Q: Can I convert other formats to MP3?
A: Yes — the audio converter accepts FLAC, M4A/AAC, OGG, OPUS, and more. Use the general audio converter tool.
Q: Is there a file-size limit?
A: Reasonable file sizes are accepted. For very long recordings, consider trimming first.
